newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche bemoans Germany's lack of venture capital.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche bemoans Germany's lack of venture capital.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG said on Monday it was providing more start-up money for innovative technology firms but warned that big reforms were needed to ensure an adequate flow of venture capital in Germany.
The bank said it set up a risk capital fund which initially has a volume of 25 million marks ($14.4 million) and will be increased by a further 20 million marks later.
Deutsche said companies trying to establish themselves in growth sectors like biotechnology, multimedia and computers suffered from an "enormous misallocation" of available capital.
The lack of pension funds in Germany was mainly to blame for the dearth of risk capital, it said.
Regulatory hurdles and tax disincentives had to be removed to allow such funds to assume the leading role as equity investors that they enjoyed in other countries.
"Without these pension funds there will no real breakthrough for risk capital," management board member Carl-Ludwig von Boehm-Bezing told a news conference.
"It is abstruse to think that we will change from a high-wage country to a low-wage country. Only innovations will safeguard Germany as a production site."

In 1995, the assets of pension funds in Germany accounted for just six percent of gross domestic product (GDP), compared with 61 percent in the U.S. and 80 percent and more in Britain, the Netherlands and Switzerland.
U.S. pension funds invested 52 percent of their assets in equities, compared with 80 percent in Britain, 26 percent in Japan and 11 percent in Germany.
"We must change the rules," Boehm-Bezing said. "Pension fund managers would be in competition for high performing stocks and that means they would invest in innovative companies."
Venture capital investment refers to providing funds for new firms in return for a shareholding and a say in management.
It is risky and the only return it offers is the income from the eventual sale of the stake. While most start-ups fail, the proceeds from the ones that succeed can be substantial.

One hurdle to the creation of pension funds in Germany is that companies' allocations to internal pension reserves are tax exempt, whereas contributions by employers and workers to external pension funds are not.
Deutsche in 1996 started a programme to promote technology companies which had already successfully launched their products and were seeking to expand.
It already has stakes worth 31 million marks in 16 companies, at least one of which is a candidate for a stock market listing.
The bank has also published brochures on managing new innovative companies and has hosted conferences and competitions over the past year.
